title: Finding Her Voice
subtitle: Maya's first presentation at work.
paras: Six months into her new job, Maya was asked to give a presentation to the whole department. The idea terrified her. Although her English was now fluent, she worried about her pronunciation, and she knew that nerves could make her rush in front of an audience. A friend who had studied psychology told her that the fear of speaking publicly is one of the most common fears there is.

So Maya signed up for an evening course in public speaking — not exactly her idea of leisure, but she was determined. The group met on the twelfth floor of an old office building, and within the first hour she began to recognise her own habits in other people: speaking without pauses, swallowing the ends of sentences, and apologising before every point.

The tutor, a former actor, was calm and thoroughly professional. He showed them how to find the natural rhythm of a sentence and to stress only the words that mattered. When one student tried to interrupt him to ask whether notes were allowed, he smiled and said notes were fine, as long as nobody read from them. Maya realised that the others had fears very similar to her own, which was strangely comforting.

By the final week, the change in her delivery was noticeable. She made sure every example was relevant to the people listening, and she had learned to treat her accent as a strength rather than a weakness. On the day itself, the room felt oddly familiar, as if she had rehearsed the moment a hundred times — which, in a way, she had.
discuss: Why was Maya so nervous, and what actually helped her? Think of a time you had to speak in front of other people. What would you do differently now?

items.clue: the way a word is said
items.trick: PRONOUNCE loses its O: pro-NUN-ciation. There is a NUN inside.

items.clue: the people who watch or listen to a talk or show
items.trick: AU + DI + ENCE. It ends in -ENCE, like silENCE, which is what you want from them.

items.clue: the scientific study of the mind and behaviour
items.trick: The P at the start is silent, and CH sounds like K.

items.clue: in front of other people; openly
free time for things you enjoy
items.trick: L-E-I at the start, then SURE. Relax, you are SURE to enjoy your LEIsure.
TWELVE changes its V to F, and the F stays: T-W-E-L-F-T-H.

items.clue: to know someone or something because you have seen it before
items.trick: There is a COG in reCOGnise. British spelling ends in -ISE (American: -IZE).

items.clue: doing a job with skill and serious standards
a regular, repeated pattern of sounds or beats
items.trick: No normal vowels at all. Remember: Rhythm Helps Your Two Hips Move.

items.clue: to stop someone while they are speaking
items.trick: Two Rs in the middle. You INTER-RUPT: the Rs crash into each other.

items.clue: if (used when there are two possibilities)
items.trick: The one meaning IF has an H. The one about rain and sun has an A.

items.clue: almost the same as something else
items.trick: One M, one L, and it ends in -AR.
NOTICE + ABLE. Keep the E so the C still sounds like S.

items.clue: connected to the subject you are discussing
items.trick: It ends in -ANT. A relevANT point is small but important, like an ANT.
STRONG keeps its G: STRENG + TH.

items.clue: well known to you because you have seen it often
items.trick: It ends in -IAR: a LIAR is hiding at the end of famiLIAR.
